models.name: Qwen3.8-27B (MLX-Serve 26.10.1)
models.full_name: Qwen3.8-27B 4-bit on MLX-Serve 26.10.1 with a DFlash-style drafter
models.why: 26.10.1 picks MTP over the DFlash drafter by default, which made the build about 2x slower on an M4 Max, so the benchmark runs it with --no-mtp: mlx-serve lands at 115 t/s on code and 54 on a story workload, within a few t/s of TensorFold and oMLX on the same weights.

engines.quant: ddalcu's 4-bit Qwen3.8-27B, drafting on, story workload

models.name: Qwen3.8-27B (MLX-Serve 26.10.1, drafter on)
models.full_name: Qwen3.8-27B 4-bit on MLX-Serve 26.10.1 with its drafter (M4 Max)
models.why: Three Apple-Silicon engines on one Qwen3.8-27B 4-bit model and one drafter land within a few t/s of each other: TensorFold 154 t/s on numbers, mlx-serve 115 on code and 54 on a story workload, and all three fall to 29-31 t/s with drafting off, so the race is the drafter, not the engine.

models.name: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125B (MLX-Serve 26.10.1)
models.full_name: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125B served by MLX-Serve 26.10.1 on Apple Silicon
models.why: The 26.10.1 release lifts Qwen Flash Next by +11 percent decode on an M4 Max and +51 percent prefill on an M5 Ultra (up to about 5,400 prompt tokens/s), and GGUF models now run on mlx-serve's own Zig/Metal engine instead of falling back to llama.cpp.

engines.hardware: Apple M5 Ultra (prefill, up to ~5,400 PP)
engines.quant: Qwen Flash Next, prefill uplift over 26.9.6 (+51%), drafting on by default
